_comment:
RFC 7518 (JSON Web Algorithms) scoped to github.com/iscultas/jwt-go, which implements the twelve JWS algorithms of section 3, all sixteen key management algorithms of section 4, and all six content encryption algorithms of section 5.

One of the sixteen is asymmetric. **RSA1_5** (section 4.2) decrypts and never encrypts, and it is not among the algorithms jwt.DefaultDecryptionConfig accepts, so neither a producer nor a default consumer reaches it. The shape rests on text the RFCs supply rather than on preference. RFC 8725 section 3.2 -- a BCP that formally updates RFC 7519 -- asks applications to avoid all RSA-PKCS1 v1.5 encryption algorithms, preferring RSAES-OAEP, which is what the two halves above do; RFC 7519 section 8 states an unqualified MUST for RSA1_5 once an implementation provides encryption, which the decrypting half meets on its own terms; and RFC 7516 section 11.4 describes the concrete attack, an "alg" rewritten from RSA-OAEP to RSA1_5 to turn the recipient into a decryption oracle, which section 11.5's substituted random CEK closes.

The algorithm was absent altogether until that reading was worked through, and the cost of the absence is what settled it: RFC 7519 section 8 went unmet, and RFC 7516 Appendix A.2, RFC 7520 section 5.1 and one recipient each of RFC 7516 Appendix A.4 and RFC 7520 section 5.13 were unreadable. All four decrypt now. See RFC7518-S4_2-R01, RFC7519-S8-R05, RFC7516-S11_4-R01, RFC7516-S11_5-R01 and RFC8725-S3_2-R06.

Three primitives in sections 4 and 5 are composed here rather than delegated, because the Go standard library provides none of them: AES_CBC_HMAC_SHA2 (section 5.2), AES Key Wrap (RFC 3394, used by section 4.4) and the Concat KDF (NIST SP 800-56A section 5.8.1, used by section 4.6.2). All three are self-consistent when implemented wrongly -- two copies of a broken implementation agree with each other and with nobody else -- so each is pinned to published arithmetic rather than to a round trip: RFC 7518 Appendix B, RFC 3394 section 4, and RFC 7518 Appendix C respectively.

Sections 6.1 ("kty" values), 7 (IANA) and the advisory subsections of 8 are recorded in `sections` with reasons. Section 8.4's 2^32 invocation limit and section 9's PRECIS password preparation are enriched as not-testable with rationales rather than dropped: the first needs per-key state this module deliberately does not hold, the second needs Unicode tables a zero-dependency module cannot carry, and both are the application's rather than the library's.

Re-enriching sections 4 and 5 -- which were excluded wholesale while this module was signature-only -- surfaced four defects, each now fixed and each covered by the requirement that found it: apu and apv were not required to be distinct (RFC7518-S4_6_2-R01); a "p2c" below the recommended floor of 1000 was accepted (RFC7518-S4_8_1_2-R02); a password of any length was accepted when producing (RFC7518-S8_8-R01); and an "epk" carrying private key material was accepted when consuming (RFC7518-S4_6_1_1-R01).

source.text: The octet sequence MUST utilize the minimum number of octets needed to represent the value.

requirements.behavior: encode a Base64urlUInt value using the fewest octets that represent it, with no leading zero octet
requirements.observable_effect: jwk.Key.MarshalJSON writes RSA n and e, and the EC coordinates, with no leading zero octet: e for the usual public exponent 65537 is exactly the three octets [1, 0, 1], which base64url-encodes to "AQAB"
requirements.oracle: Marshal an RSA jwk.Key and base64url-decode its e and n members. e must decode to exactly [1, 0, 1] for the 65537 exponent crypto/rsa generates by default, and n's first octet must be non-zero. The e case is the one the RFC spells out itself in section 6.3.1.2, so it doubles as that requirement's test vector.
inputs: an RSA key with the default 65537 public exponent

notes: Base64urlUInt is defined in section 2 but only ever applied in section 6; the two are tested together because the encoding is observable nowhere else.

source.text: The table below is the set of "alg" (algorithm) Header Parameter values defined by this specification for use with JWS, each of which is explained in more detail in the following sections: | HS256 | HMAC using SHA-256 | Required | ... | RS256 | RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 using SHA-256 | Recommended | ES256 | ECDSA using P-256 and SHA-256 | Recommended+ | ... | none | No digital signature or MAC performed | Optional |

requirements.behavior: implement HS256, whose Implementation Requirements entry is Required
requirements.observable_effect: jwa.ByName("HS256") resolves, and the algorithm it returns both signs and verifies

compound_review.rationale: no keywords at all; the sentence is the algorithm table, long by shape rather than by compound obligation, and its Required, Recommended and Optional levels are already minted as this requirement's two siblings

requirements.oracle: jwa.ByName("HS256") returns an algorithm implementing both jwa.Signer and jwa.Verifier, and a round trip through Sign then Verify succeeds. Required is the strongest entry in the table's Implementation Requirements column, so it is read as a MUST.

notes: Promoted: the table states implementation strength in its own column vocabulary (Required / Recommended / Recommended+ / Optional) rather than in BCP 14 keywords. Required is mapped to MUST, Recommended and Recommended+ to SHOULD, and Optional to MAY.

source_review.reason: The opening sentence is verbatim; the section's algorithm table follows it rendered as rows joined with " | " and abridged with "...", since a table cannot be a substring of the document.

requirements.behavior: implement RS256 and ES256, whose Implementation Requirements entries are Recommended and Recommended+
requirements.observable_effect: jwa.ByName resolves both "RS256" and "ES256", and each signs and verifies

compound_review.rationale: no keywords at all; the sentence is the algorithm table, long by shape rather than by compound obligation, and its Required, Recommended and Optional levels are already minted as this requirement's two siblings

requirements.oracle: jwa.ByName resolves RS256 and ES256 and each round-trips through Sign then Verify. The "+" on ES256 marks a requirement strength the specification expects to raise later, which is a reason to implement it rather than a stronger obligation today.

notes: Promoted from the Implementation Requirements column, as for -R01.

requirements.behavior: implement any of the algorithms marked Optional, or none of them
requirements.observable_effect: the nine Optional identifiers -- HS384, HS512, RS384, RS512, ES384, ES512, PS256, PS384, PS512 -- and "none" all resolve through jwa.ByName in this implementation, which is conformant but not required; an implementation resolving none of them would be equally conformant

compound_review.rationale: no keywords at all; the sentence is the algorithm table, long by shape rather than by compound obligation, and its Required, Recommended and Optional levels are already minted as this requirement's two siblings

requirements.oracle: For each Optional identifier, jwa.ByName either resolves it to a working algorithm or reports it unsupported; both outcomes are conformant. What must hold either way is that an unresolved identifier produces jwa.ErrUnsupportedAlgorithm rather than a silent fallback, since a recipient that quietly substitutes an algorithm it does understand for one it does not is the failure this optionality would otherwise invite.
inputs: each Optional alg identifier from the section 3.1 table

notes: Promoted from the Implementation Requirements column, as for -R01.

source.text: A key of the same size as the hash output (for instance, 256 bits for "HS256") or larger MUST be used with this algorithm.

requirements.behavior: use an HMAC key at least as large as the hash output
requirements.observable_effect: jwa.HMACSHA2.Sign and .Verify return jwa.ErrWeakKey for a secret shorter than the hash output -- 32 octets for HS256, 48 for HS384, 64 for HS512 -- and accept one of exactly that size
requirements.oracle: For each of HS256/HS384/HS512, signing and verifying with a secret one octet short of the hash output size returns an error wrapping jwa.ErrWeakKey, and a secret of exactly that size is accepted. Checking the boundary from both sides is what distinguishes a real minimum from a check that rejects everything or nothing.
inputs: a secret of exactly hash.Size() octets
errata: eid8568 (Verified, editorial): corrects the NIST citation supporting this requirement from SP 800-117 to SP 800-107. It does not change the requirement.

notes: Verified against the implementation before this oracle was written: prior to the fix landed with this suite, a one-octet secret signed and verified under all three algorithms.

Enforced on verification as well as signing. The RFC binds use of the algorithm rather than production alone, and a verifier accepting an undersized key accepts a MAC cheaper to forge than its alg advertises.

source.text: The comparison of the computed HMAC value to the JWS Signature value MUST be done in a constant-time manner to thwart timing attacks.

requirements.behavior: compare a computed HMAC against the received signature in constant time
requirements.observable_effect: jwa.HMACSHA2.Verify compares with crypto/hmac.Equal rather than bytes.Equal or ==
requirements.oracle: Read jwa/hmac_sha_2.go and assert the comparison is hmac.Equal, and that no non-constant-time comparison of the MAC appears. A timing measurement would be the direct oracle but is not dependable inside a Go test process, so the source-level check stands in for it -- the same approach the RFC 7515 suite takes for its section 10.9 requirement.

notes: Shares its oracle with RFC7515-S10_9-R01, which states the same obligation. Tested here as well because the requirement is stated independently in each RFC.

source.text: A key of size 2048 bits or larger MUST be used with these algorithms.

requirements.behavior: use an RSA key of at least 2048 bits with the RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 algorithms
requirements.observable_effect: the RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 Sign and Verify methods return jwa.ErrWeakKey for a key whose modulus is under 2048 bits, and accept one of exactly 2048
requirements.oracle: Signing and verifying with a 1024-bit RSA key under each RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 algorithm returns an error wrapping jwa.ErrWeakKey, while a 2048-bit key succeeds. 1024 rather than 512 is deliberate: crypto/rsa refuses to generate anything below 1024, so 1024 is the largest non-conformant key the standard library will produce.

notes: Verified before the oracle was written: a 1024-bit key signed and verified under both families prior to the fix landed with this suite.

source.text: The octet sequence representations MUST NOT be shortened to omit any leading zero octets contained in the values.

requirements.behavior: not shorten the octet representation of R or S to omit leading zero octets
requirements.observable_effect: every signature jwa.ECDSA.Sign produces is exactly twice the curve's coordinate width, whatever the values of R and S; a leading zero in either is padded rather than dropped
requirements.oracle: Sign repeatedly with a P-256 key and assert every signature is exactly 64 octets. R and S are uniform over the curve order, so a run of a few hundred signatures makes a value with a leading zero octet overwhelmingly likely (about a 1-in-256 chance each), and a shortening implementation would emit a 63-octet signature for one of them. The invariant is what is asserted; the RFC's prohibition is not otherwise observable from outside.
inputs: several hundred P-256 signatures over varying inputs
errata: eid6612 (Verified, editorial): fixes "being be 32 octets long" to "being 32 octets long" in this section's step 2. No change to the requirement.

notes: The implementation uses big.Int.FillBytes into a fixed-width buffer, which cannot shorten. The property test is written to hold whatever the implementation, not to mirror it.

source.text: The JWS Signature value MUST be a 64-octet sequence.

requirements.behavior: treat an ES256 JWS Signature value as valid only when it is a 64-octet sequence
requirements.observable_effect: jwa.ES256().Verify rejects any signature that is not 64 octets, and jwa.ES256().Sign never produces one of another length because it refuses every key not on P-256
requirements.oracle: ES256 verification of a 63- and a 65-octet signature returns jwa.ErrMalformedSignature. Signing with a P-256 key yields exactly 64 octets. Signing with a P-384 or P-521 key -- which would otherwise yield 96 or 132 octets and so break this rule -- is refused outright; see -R03.

source.text: This specification defines the use of ECDSA with the P-256 curve and the SHA-256 cryptographic hash function, ECDSA with the P-384 curve and the SHA-384 hash function, and ECDSA with the P-521 curve and the SHA-512 hash function. ... | ES256 | ECDSA using P-256 and SHA-256 | ES384 | ECDSA using P-384 and SHA-384 | ES512 | ECDSA using P-521 and SHA-512 |

requirements.behavior: use each ECDSA algorithm identifier only with the one curve it names
requirements.observable_effect: jwa.ES256/ES384/ES512 accept keys on P-256/P-384/P-521 respectively and return jwa.ErrInvalidKeyType for a key on any other curve, in both Sign and Verify
requirements.oracle: For each of the nine algorithm-curve combinations, signing and verifying succeed on the three matched pairs and return an error wrapping jwa.ErrInvalidKeyType on the six mismatched ones. The matched cases additionally produce signatures of 64, 96 and 132 octets, which is the same fact section 3.4 states as a length rule.
inputs: each of ES256, ES384 and ES512

notes: Promoted: the pairing is stated in prose and again in the section 3.1 table, in both cases without a BCP 14 keyword, yet it is what the keyworded length rule in -R02 depends on.
Verified before the oracle was written: prior to the fix landed with this suite, ES256 signed with a P-521 key and emitted a 132-octet signature, which -R02 forbids.

source_review.reason: The two prose sentences are verbatim; the curve-to-algorithm table follows them rendered as rows joined with " | ", which no rendering of a table can make substring-findable.

source.text: For ECDSA P-384 SHA-384, R and S will be 384 bits each, resulting in a 96-octet sequence. For ECDSA P-521 SHA-512, R and S will be 521 bits each, resulting in a 132-octet sequence.

requirements.behavior: produce and require a 96-octet signature for ES384 and a 132-octet signature for ES512
requirements.observable_effect: jwa.ES384 signs to exactly 96 octets and jwa.ES512 to exactly 132, and each rejects a signature of any other length
requirements.oracle: ES384 over a P-384 key produces 96 octets and ES512 over a P-521 key produces 132; a signature one octet shorter or longer is rejected with jwa.ErrMalformedSignature. The 132 figure is the one worth asserting explicitly: P-521's 521-bit coordinates round up to 66 octets each rather than the 65 a naive division would give.

notes: Promoted: stated in prose as a consequence of the ES256 procedure, with no keyword.

source.text: A key of size 2048 bits or larger MUST be used with this algorithm.

requirements.behavior: use an RSA key of at least 2048 bits with the RSASSA-PSS algorithms
requirements.observable_effect: the RSASSA-PSS Sign and Verify methods return jwa.ErrWeakKey for a key whose modulus is under 2048 bits, and accept one of exactly 2048
requirements.oracle: Signing and verifying with a 1024-bit RSA key under each RSASSA-PSS algorithm returns an error wrapping jwa.ErrWeakKey, while a 2048-bit key succeeds. 1024 rather than 512 is deliberate: crypto/rsa refuses to generate anything below 1024, so 1024 is the largest non-conformant key the standard library will produce.

notes: Verified before the oracle was written: a 1024-bit key signed and verified under both families prior to the fix landed with this suite.

source.text: This section defines the use of the RSASSA-PSS digital signature algorithm as defined in Section 8.1 of RFC 3447 [RFC3447] with the MGF1 mask generation function and SHA-2 hash functions, always using the same hash function for both the RSASSA-PSS hash function and the MGF1 hash function.  The size of the salt value is the same size as the hash function output.

requirements.behavior: sign with MGF1 and a salt of the same length as the hash output
requirements.observable_effect: a signature from jwa.RSASSAPSS.Sign verifies under crypto/rsa.VerifyPSS with SaltLength set to rsa.PSSSaltLengthEqualsHash, which it would not if the salt were of any other length
requirements.oracle: Sign with each of PS256/PS384/PS512, then verify with rsa.VerifyPSS passing &rsa.PSSOptions{SaltLength: rsa.PSSSaltLengthEqualsHash}. That option makes the salt length part of what is checked, so verification succeeding is what proves the producer used it. Verification in the library itself is deliberately lenient about salt length -- the RFC binds the producer -- so the library's own Verify cannot serve as this oracle.
inputs: each of PS256, PS384 and PS512

notes: Promoted: the parameters are stated in the section's opening sentence with no keyword.

Repaired: the stored text had merged and reworded this sentence and the salt-length sentence that follows it. Both are now quoted as the section prints them; the obligation the entry tests is unchanged.

source.text: JWSs MAY also be created that do not provide integrity protection.

requirements.behavior: support the creation of a JWS that provides no integrity protection
requirements.observable_effect: jwa.None() exists and produces an unsecured JWS, which is conformant; an implementation offering no such algorithm would be equally conformant
requirements.oracle: jwa.ByName("none") resolves and jwa.None().Sign returns the empty signature. The interop half is what matters and is not skippable: whether or not an implementation can create an unsecured JWS, it must not accept one by default, which -R05 asserts.

source.text: An Unsecured JWS uses the "alg" value "none" and is formatted identically to other JWSs, but MUST use the empty octet sequence as its JWS Signature value.

requirements.behavior: use the empty octet sequence as the JWS Signature value of an unsecured JWS
requirements.observable_effect: jwa.None().Sign returns a zero-length slice, and a token signed with none serializes with an empty signature part
requirements.oracle: jwa.None().Sign returns a slice of length 0 for any input. A jwt.Token signed with jwa.None() serializes in compact form to a string whose third dot-separated part is empty.

source.text: Recipients MUST verify that the JWS Signature value is the empty octet sequence.

requirements.behavior: verify that the JWS Signature value of an unsecured JWS is the empty octet sequence
requirements.observable_effect: jwa.None().Verify reports false for any non-empty signature and true only for the empty one
requirements.oracle: jwa.None().Verify returns true for a zero-length signature and false for a non-empty one. A token naming alg=none but carrying signature octets must therefore fail verification even when the caller has explicitly allowed none.

notes: Verified before the oracle was written: prior to the fix landed with this suite, NoneAlgorithm.Verify returned true unconditionally, so a token naming alg=none while carrying signature octets was accepted whenever none was allowed at all.

source.text: Implementations that support Unsecured JWSs MUST NOT accept such objects as valid unless the application specifies that it is acceptable for a specific object to not be integrity protected.

requirements.condition: the implementation supports Unsecured JWSs at all
requirements.behavior: not accept an unsecured JWS as valid unless the application has said that object need not be integrity protected
requirements.observable_effect: jwt.Verify rejects a none-signed token under the default configuration and accepts it only when the caller passes jwa.None() to jwt.WithAlgorithms for that call
requirements.oracle: Verifying a none-signed token with jwt.DefaultVerificationConfig fails with jwt.ErrForbiddenAlgorithm; the same token verifies once the caller supplies jwt.WithAlgorithms(jwa.None()). The opt-in is what the RFC calls the application specifying that the object need not be protected.

source.text: Implementations MUST NOT accept Unsecured JWSs by default.

requirements.behavior: not accept unsecured JWSs by default
requirements.observable_effect: verifying a none-signed token fails with jwt.ErrForbiddenAlgorithm under the default configuration, without the caller having to exclude none
requirements.oracle: Verifying a none-signed token returns jwt.ErrForbiddenAlgorithm under jwt.DefaultVerificationConfig and under a freshly built jwt.NewVerificationConfig(). Both are checked rather than the config's algorithm list being inspected: the list is unexported, and what the rule constrains is the outcome, not the representation. Building a fresh default also catches a shared value some earlier caller had widened.

source.text: In order to mitigate downgrade attacks, applications MUST NOT signal acceptance of Unsecured JWSs at a global level, and SHOULD signal acceptance on a per-object basis.

requirements.behavior: not signal acceptance of unsecured JWSs at a global level, signalling it per object instead
requirements.observable_effect: the acceptance of none is a field of the VerificationConfig value passed to each jwt.Verify call, with no package-level setting that could turn it on for every call at once

compound_review.rationale: the MUST NOT and the SHOULD are a prohibition and the sanctioned alternative to it, one decision about where acceptance is signalled; the oracle asserts both halves

requirements.oracle: Build two configs, one allowing none and one not, and verify the same none-signed token under each in turn: the permissive one accepts and the default one still rejects. That the second is unaffected by the first is what shows acceptance is carried per call rather than held globally. The requirement is addressed to applications, but a library that offered only a global switch would make obeying it impossible, so what is tested is that the library permits per-object signalling.
inputs: a permissive config and a default config used in the same process

notes: The sentence also carries a SHOULD (signal acceptance on a per-object basis) alongside this MUST NOT. They are two statements of one arrangement rather than two obligations, so they are kept as one requirement at the stronger level.

source.text: A key of size 2048 bits or larger MUST be used with this algorithm.

requirements.condition: RSA1_5 key decryption is requested
requirements.behavior: refuse a key whose modulus is smaller than 2048 bits, before the unwrap
requirements.observable_effect: jwa.RSA15().DecryptKey returns jwa.ErrWeakKey for a 1024- or 2047-bit modulus and proceeds at 2048
requirements.oracle:
TestRSA15RequiresA2048BitModulus in conformance/rfc7518: DecryptKey with a 1024-bit and a 2047-bit key returns jwa.ErrWeakKey, and a 2048-bit key is accepted, so the floor sits where the sentence puts it rather than somewhere stricter. The same checkRSAModulus enforces sections 3.3, 3.5, 4.2 and 4.3 -- one definition of "large enough", since it is the same sentence in all four places. The check runs before the unwrap, so the encrypted key is immaterial to the outcome.

This requirement was carried as not-testable while RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 was unimplemented, when no key of any size reached it. What replaced the exclusion is a narrower position, asserted alongside the floor by TestRSA15DecryptsAndDoesNotEncrypt: the algorithm decrypts and never encrypts. jwa.RSAESPKCS1v15 has DecryptKey and neither EncryptKey nor WrapKey, so it is a jwa.KeyDecrypter and is not a jwa.KeyEncrypter, and jwe refuses it when encrypting. Reading a token another party wrote and writing a new one carry different risk; RFC 8725 section 3.2 asks applications to "Avoid all RSA-PKCS1 v1.5 encryption algorithms ..., preferring RSAES-OAEP", which is carried at RFC8725-S3_2-R06, and jwt.DefaultDecryptionConfig does not accept RSA1_5 either.

The countermeasure that makes the decryption half safe to offer is not this requirement's: it belongs to RFC 7516 sections 11.4 and 11.5, and is asserted at RFC7516-S11_4-R01 and RFC7516-S11_5-R01. RFC 7516 Appendix A.2 and RFC 7520 section 5.1 are the interop half, and both decrypt.
requirements.rationale:
RFC 7518 section 4.2 is RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 key encryption. This module implements the decrypting half of it and not the encrypting half, so the sentence applies to a real code path and the requirement is asserted rather than excluded.

It was carried as not-testable while the algorithm was absent altogether, on the strength of RFC 8725 section 3.2 -- a BCP that formally updates RFC 7519 -- together with RFC 7518 section 8.3 and RFC 7516 section 11.4's concrete attack. That position had a cost the IR recorded in two places: RFC 7519 section 8 states an unqualified MUST for RSA1_5 once an implementation provides encryption (RFC7519-S8-R05), and RFC 7516 Appendix A.2, RFC 7520 section 5.1 and one recipient each of RFC 7516 Appendix A.4 and RFC 7520 section 5.13 were unreadable. Implementing the decrypting half settles the MUST on its own terms and makes those four vectors live, while "avoid" is honoured by the two things a caller cannot override: this module writes no such token, and reads one only when asked.

source.text: A key of size 2048 bits or larger MUST be used with these algorithms.

requirements.condition: RSA-OAEP or RSA-OAEP-256 is used to encrypt a CEK
requirements.behavior: refuse a key whose modulus is smaller than 2048 bits
requirements.observable_effect: encrypting to an undersized RSA key fails with jwa.ErrWeakKey rather than producing a token
requirements.oracle: jwa.RSAOAEP().EncryptKey and RSAOAEP256().EncryptKey return jwa.ErrWeakKey for a 1024-bit or 2047-bit modulus and succeed at 2048. The check is jwa.checkRSAModulus, shared with the signing algorithms of sections 3.3 and 3.5 -- one definition of "large enough", since the floor is the same sentence in both places. Enforced when producing rather than only when consuming, because a token this module would refuse to write is not one it should be able to write by accident.

source.section_title: Key Agreement with Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral Static
source.text: A new ephemeral public key value MUST be generated for each key agreement operation.

requirements.condition: ECDH-ES key agreement is performed
requirements.behavior: generate a new ephemeral key pair for every agreement
requirements.observable_effect: two encryptions to the same recipient publish different epk values and derive different CEKs
requirements.oracle: jwa.ECDHESAlgorithm.deriveKeyEncryptionKey calls ecdsa.GenerateKey itself and never accepts an ephemeral key from the caller, which is what makes the requirement hold without the caller's cooperation. Asserted by encrypting twice to one recipient and comparing the published epk and the resulting ciphertext: both differ. Also asserted per recipient rather than per message -- two recipients of one multi-recipient JWE get different epk values -- since a reused ephemeral key turns ephemeral-static agreement into static-static and gives every message the same CEK.

source.section_title: Key Agreement with Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral Static
source.text: In Direct Key Agreement mode, the output of the Concat KDF MUST be a key of the same length as that used by the "enc" algorithm.

requirements.condition: ECDH-ES is used in Direct Key Agreement mode
requirements.behavior: make the Concat KDF output the length the "enc" algorithm uses
requirements.observable_effect: the derived CEK is exactly enc.KeySize() octets for every enc
requirements.oracle: jwa.ECDHESAlgorithm.derivedKeySize returns encryption.KeySize() when keyWrap is nil. Asserted across all six content encryption algorithms, since the whole point of the rule is that the length tracks the "enc" value rather than being fixed. Verified against RFC 7518 Appendix C, whose worked example reproduces the derived key VqqN6vgjbSBcIijNcacQGg -- the arithmetic, not just the length.

source.section_title: Key Agreement with Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral Static
source.text: In Key Agreement with Key Wrapping mode, the output of the Concat KDF MUST be a key of the length needed for the specified key wrapping algorithm.

requirements.condition: ECDH-ES is used in Key Agreement with Key Wrapping mode
requirements.behavior: make the Concat KDF output the length the named key wrapping algorithm needs
requirements.observable_effect: ECDH-ES+A128KW derives 16 octets, +A192KW 24 and +A256KW 32, whatever the enc
requirements.oracle:
jwa.ECDHESAlgorithm.derivedKeySize returns keyWrap.keySize when a wrapping algorithm is present, and encryption.KeySize() when there is none. That is asserted directly by jwa's internal TestECDHESDerivesTheWrappingKeySize, because the derived key never surfaces through the public API -- it is consumed by the wrapping step -- and a round trip cannot pin its length: a wrapping key of the wrong length would be accepted by aes.NewCipher as a different AES variant and both sides would derive it identically.

conformance/rfc7518 adds the observable consequence across the cross product of the three wrapping variants and the six enc algorithms: the CEK follows the "enc", the encrypted key is the CEK plus AES-KW's one extra semiblock, and the pairing round-trips. That is what would break if this rule and RFC7518-S4_6-R02's were swapped, which is the mistake worth guarding against.

The two modes must also not derive the same key from one agreement, which is what the AlgorithmID rule of section 4.6.2 is for; jwa's TestECDHESSeparatesItsTwoModes asserts that with a guard that both modes derive the same length, so it cannot pass merely because the outputs differ in size.
inputs: each wrapping variant against each enc
derivedKeySize called directly in both modes

source.text: It MUST contain only public key parameters and SHOULD contain only the minimum JWK parameters necessary to represent the key; other JWK parameters included can be checked for consistency and honored, or they can be ignored.

requirements.condition: an "epk" Header Parameter is produced or consumed
requirements.behavior: carry only public key parameters in it
requirements.observable_effect: a published epk holds only kty, crv, x and y; a received one carrying d is refused

compound_review.rationale: the SHOULD narrows the MUST rather than adding to it -- public parameters only, and minimally so -- and the oracle asserts the minimum explicitly

requirements.oracle:
Both directions, because they fail differently.

Producing: header.SetKeyParameters routes the ephemeral key through jwk.Key.Public, which strips the private half, and the encoded epk carries exactly kty, crv, x and y -- the minimum this sentence's SHOULD asks for as well. A private key handed to it is published as its public half rather than rejected, since the caller supplying a private key is supplying the right thing and only the public half is publishable.

Consuming: header.UnmarshalJSON returns header.ErrPrivateEphemeralKey for an epk carrying d. This was a real gap found while re-enriching this section -- such a header previously decoded to an *ecdsa.PrivateKey and the agreement proceeded from its public half. The agreement would have derived the correct key, so this is not about a wrong result: it is that the private half changes the key's JWK thumbprint, so implementations disagreeing about whether to strip it would disagree about the key's identity, and a sender who leaked their ephemeral private key deserves an error rather than accommodation.
inputs: a private ephemeral key on the producing side

notes: multiple keywords in one sentence; split into one requirement each

source.text: This Header Parameter MUST be present and MUST be understood and processed by implementations when these algorithms are used.

requirements.condition: ECDH-ES or one of its key wrapping variants is used
requirements.behavior: require "epk" to be present, and process it
requirements.observable_effect: a JWE naming ECDH-ES with no epk fails to decrypt

compound_review.rationale: presence and processing are one obligation on the receiver, and the oracle asserts both: epk absent fails, and a peer's epk is actually used

requirements.oracle: jwa.ECDHESAlgorithm.DecryptKey returns an error when parameters.EphemeralPublicKey is nil, for all four variants. It is processed rather than merely required: the RFC 7520 section 5.5 vector, whose epk was produced by another implementation, decrypts to the published plaintext.
inputs: a header naming ECDH-ES with no epk

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

source.text: Use of this Header Parameter is OPTIONAL.

requirements.condition: an "apu" value is available
requirements.behavior: the parameter may be used or omitted
requirements.observable_effect: messages with and without apu both round-trip
requirements.oracle: Encrypting under ECDH-ES with apu set and with it absent both round-trip, and the two derive different keys -- which is the interop obligation behind the option: an implementation that accepted an apu and then ignored it would decrypt to garbage, so omitting the parameter and ignoring it are not the same thing. jwa.concatKDF length-prefixes the value, so an absent apu contributes a zero length rather than nothing at all.

notes: short REQUIRED/OPTIONAL usage; often a field-table label rather than a requirement

source.text: This Header Parameter MUST be understood and processed by implementations when these algorithms are used.

requirements.condition: an "apu" is present on a JWE using ECDH-ES
requirements.behavior: feed it to the Concat KDF as PartyUInfo
requirements.observable_effect: changing apu changes the derived key, so a recipient that ignored it would fail to decrypt
requirements.oracle: Decrypting a message whose apu has been altered by one octet fails. This is the assertion that distinguishes processing the parameter from merely accepting it: an implementation that dropped apu would pass any test that only ever set it consistently on both sides.
inputs: a message whose apu was altered after encryption

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

source.text: Use of this Header Parameter is OPTIONAL.

requirements.condition: an "apv" value is available
requirements.behavior: the parameter may be used or omitted
requirements.observable_effect: messages with and without apv both round-trip
requirements.oracle: As RFC7518-S4_6_1_2-R01, for PartyVInfo. Both are asserted, since a KDF implementation that fed one value into both slots would satisfy either alone.

notes: short REQUIRED/OPTIONAL usage; often a field-table label rather than a requirement

source.text: This Header Parameter MUST be understood and processed by implementations when these algorithms are used.

requirements.condition: an "apv" is present on a JWE using ECDH-ES
requirements.behavior: feed it to the Concat KDF as PartyVInfo
requirements.observable_effect: changing apv changes the derived key
requirements.oracle: As RFC7518-S4_6_1_2-R02, for apv. Altering it by one octet makes decryption fail.
inputs: a message whose apv was altered after encryption

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

source.section_title: Key Derivation for ECDH Key Agreement
source.text: The "apu" and "apv" values MUST be distinct, when used.

requirements.condition: both "apu" and "apv" are used
requirements.behavior: require them to be distinct
requirements.observable_effect: a message setting both to the same value is refused, in both directions
requirements.oracle:
jwa.ECDHESAlgorithm.agree returns jwa.ErrIndistinctAgreementParties when apu and apv carry equal non-empty values, on both the encrypting and decrypting paths. This was a real gap found while re-enriching this section: equal values were previously accepted and fed to the KDF.

The condition is "when used": two absent values are not two equal ones, and sections 4.6.1.2 and 4.6.1.3 make both optional, so the check applies only when apu is non-empty. Both boundaries are asserted -- equal values refused, distinct values and both-absent accepted -- so the test cannot pass by refusing everything.

The rule has a reason: PartyUInfo and PartyVInfo exist to bind the derived key to who each side is, and equal values make the two contributions interchangeable and the binding vacuous.

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

source.section_title: Key Derivation for ECDH Key Agreement
source.text: Alternatively, applications MAY conduct key derivation in a manner similar to "Diffie-Hellman Key Agreement Method" [RFC2631]: in that case, the "apu" parameter MAY either be omitted or represent a random 512-bit value (analogous to PartyAInfo in Ephemeral-Static mode in RFC 2631) and the "apv" parameter SHOULD NOT be present.

requirements.condition: an application prefers RFC 2631's key derivation conventions
requirements.behavior: it may omit apu or set it to a random 512-bit value
requirements.observable_effect: this module imposes no policy on the values: any octet string a caller supplies is carried and fed to the KDF unchanged

compound_review.rationale: all three keywords describe one optional derivation mode the application owns; the apv clause applies only inside that mode, which this library does not implement

requirements.oracle: A 512-bit random apu round-trips and derives a key distinct from the same message with apu absent. The permission is the application's to exercise and this module's obligation is only not to obstruct it, which is what is asserted: no length is imposed, no value is rejected except the equality of RFC7518-S4_6_2-R01, and the octets reach the KDF as given.

notes: multiple keywords in one sentence; split into one requirement each

source.text: Use of an Initialization Vector (IV) of size 96 bits is REQUIRED with this algorithm.

requirements.condition: AES GCM key wrapping is used
requirements.behavior: use a 96-bit initialization vector
requirements.observable_effect: the published "iv" Header Parameter is 12 octets for all three A*GCMKW algorithms
requirements.oracle: jwa.AESGCMKeyWrap.WrapKey draws exactly gcmIVSize (12) octets and writes them to parameters.InitializationVector, for A128GCMKW, A192GCMKW and A256GCMKW alike. Drawn internally rather than taken from the caller, which is what makes the length unconditional and also stops an IV being supplied twice -- see RFC7518-S8_4-R02. A received iv of any other length fails to decrypt.
inputs: a received iv of 11 and 13 octets

source.text: The requested size of the Authentication Tag output MUST be 128 bits, regardless of the key size.

requirements.condition: AES GCM key wrapping is used
requirements.behavior: request a 128-bit authentication tag regardless of key size
requirements.observable_effect: the published "tag" Header Parameter is 16 octets for all three A*GCMKW algorithms
requirements.oracle: jwa.AESGCMKeyWrap.WrapKey splits the sealed output at gcmTagSize (16) octets from the end and publishes that as the tag, for all three key sizes. "Regardless of the key size" is the operative clause and is why all three are asserted rather than one: the tag length does not scale with the key, and an implementation that assumed it did would still interoperate with itself.

source.text: This Header Parameter MUST be present and MUST be understood and processed by implementations when these algorithms are used.

requirements.condition: one of the AES GCM key wrapping algorithms is used
requirements.behavior: require the "iv" Header Parameter to be present, and process it
requirements.observable_effect: a JWE naming A128GCMKW with no iv fails to decrypt

compound_review.rationale: presence and processing are one obligation on the receiver, and the oracle asserts both: iv absent fails, and altering a present iv fails too

requirements.oracle: jwa.AESGCMKeyWrap.DecryptKey fails when parameters.InitializationVector is absent or the wrong length. Processed rather than merely required: altering the published iv by one octet makes the unwrap fail, which an implementation that read the parameter and then used its own would not do.
inputs: a header naming A128GCMKW with no iv

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

source.text: This Header Parameter MUST be present and MUST be understood and processed by implementations when these algorithms are used.

requirements.condition: one of the AES GCM key wrapping algorithms is used
requirements.behavior: require the "tag" Header Parameter to be present, and process it
requirements.observable_effect: a JWE naming A128GCMKW with no tag, or with an altered one, fails to decrypt

compound_review.rationale: presence and processing are one obligation on the receiver, and the oracle asserts both: tag absent fails, and every octet of a present tag is walked

requirements.oracle: jwa.AESGCMKeyWrap.DecryptKey rejoins the encrypted key with parameters.AuthenticationTag before opening the AEAD, so an absent or altered tag fails with jwa.ErrDecryptionFailed. Every octet of the tag is walked rather than only the first, for the reason given at RFC7516-S11_5-R01: a comparison checking a prefix would be caught by a flip at octet zero and by nothing else.
inputs: a header naming A128GCMKW with no tag
every octet of the tag flipped in turn

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

source.text: The PBES2 password input is an octet sequence; if the password to be used is represented as a text string rather than an octet sequence, the UTF-8 encoding of the text string MUST be used as the octet sequence.

requirements.condition: the password to be used is a text string rather than an octet sequence
requirements.behavior: use its UTF-8 encoding as the octet sequence
requirements.observable_effect: this module's API takes []byte, so the encoding is the caller's and is not guessed

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

requirements.rationale: jwa.PBES2 takes the password as []byte and never as a string, so there is no point at which this module chooses an encoding -- the requirement is discharged by the API shape rather than by a code path a test could exercise. That is the right division: Go source is UTF-8, so []byte(s) of a Go string is already the UTF-8 encoding this sentence asks for, and a library that accepted a string would be making the caller's normalization decisions for them. See RFC7518-S9-R01 for the preparation step that precedes this one. It is also not-testable, but on separate ground -- PRECIS needs Unicode tables this module will not carry -- so it is cited as a neighbouring finding and is not what this exclusion rests on.

source.text: The salt parameter MUST be computed from the "p2s" (PBES2 salt input) Header Parameter value and the "alg" (algorithm) Header Parameter value as specified in the "p2s" definition below.

requirements.condition: PBES2 derives a key encryption key
requirements.behavior: compute the salt as UTF8(Alg) || 0x00 || the "p2s" value
requirements.observable_effect: one password and one salt input derive different keys under the three PBES2 algorithms
requirements.oracle: jwa.PBES2.derive builds the salt as slices.Concat([]byte(algorithm.name), []byte{0}, parameters.PBES2SaltInput). Asserted by deriving with one password and one salt input under all three algorithms and requiring the three results to be pairwise different -- which the algorithm-name prefix is what produces. Without it, work done against a token using one algorithm would carry to the others, and the test would pass on a naive implementation that used the salt input alone.
inputs: one password and salt input across the three PBES2 algorithms

source.text: The iteration count parameter MUST be provided as the "p2c" (PBES2 count) Header Parameter value.

requirements.condition: PBES2 derives a key encryption key
requirements.behavior: take the iteration count from the "p2c" Header Parameter
requirements.observable_effect: changing p2c changes the derived key, so a recipient using its own count would fail
requirements.oracle: Decrypting a message whose p2c has been changed after encryption fails. The count is read from the header rather than from a constant, which is what makes the parameter meaningful -- and is also why it is bounded in both directions; see RFC7518-S4_8_1_2-R02.
inputs: a message whose p2c was altered after encryption

source.text: This Header Parameter MUST be present and MUST be understood and processed by implementations when these algorithms are used.

requirements.condition: one of the PBES2 algorithms is used
requirements.behavior: require the "p2s" Header Parameter to be present, and process it
requirements.observable_effect: a JWE naming PBES2 with no p2s fails to decrypt, and altering p2s makes it fail

compound_review.rationale: presence and processing are one obligation on the receiver, and the oracle asserts both: p2s absent fails, and altering a present p2s fails too

requirements.oracle: jwa.PBES2.derive fails when parameters.PBES2SaltInput is shorter than the minimum, which an absent one is. Altering a present p2s by one octet also fails, which is the half that shows it is processed rather than merely required.
inputs: a header naming PBES2 with no p2s

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

source.text: A Salt Input value containing 8 or more octets MUST be used.

requirements.condition: a PBES2 salt input is supplied or received
requirements.behavior: require at least 8 octets
requirements.observable_effect: a p2s of 7 octets is refused; 8 is accepted
requirements.oracle: jwa.PBES2.derive returns jwa.ErrInvalidKeySize for a salt input below minimumPBES2SaltInputSize (8). Both sides of the boundary are asserted -- 7 refused, 8 accepted -- so the test cannot pass by refusing every length. This module generates 16 octets of its own, comfortably above the floor, since the salt costs nothing and its whole job is to make one precomputed table useless against a second token.

source.text: A new Salt Input value MUST be generated randomly for every encryption operation; see RFC 4086 [RFC4086] for considerations on generating random values.

requirements.condition: PBES2 encrypts a key
requirements.behavior: generate a new salt input randomly for every encryption operation
requirements.observable_effect: two encryptions under one password publish different p2s values
requirements.oracle: jwa.PBES2.WrapKey draws the salt input from crypto/rand itself and overwrites whatever the caller supplied, which is what makes the requirement hold without the caller's cooperation. Asserted by encrypting twice under one password and comparing the published p2s. Also per call rather than per message: two recipients of one multi-recipient JWE receive different salts, which is the case a per-message implementation would get wrong.

source.text: This Header Parameter MUST be present and MUST be understood and processed by implementations when these algorithms are used.

requirements.condition: one of the PBES2 algorithms is used
requirements.behavior: require the "p2c" Header Parameter to be present, and process it
requirements.observable_effect: a JWE naming PBES2 with no p2c fails to decrypt

compound_review.rationale: presence and processing are one obligation on the receiver, and the oracle asserts both: p2c absent fails, and the count read from the header is the count used

requirements.oracle: An absent p2c decodes as zero, which jwa.PBES2.derive refuses with jwa.ErrInsufficientIterationCount. Processed rather than merely required, per RFC7518-S4_8-R03: the count read from the header is the count used.
inputs: a header naming PBES2 with no p2c

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

source.text: A minimum iteration count of 1000 is RECOMMENDED.

requirements.condition: a "p2c" iteration count is supplied or received
requirements.behavior: use at least 1000
requirements.observable_effect: a p2c below 1000 is refused; the count this module writes is 600,000
requirements.oracle:
jwa.PBES2.derive returns jwa.ErrInsufficientIterationCount below minimumPBES2Count (1000) and accepts 1000 exactly, so the boundary is where the RFC puts it. This was a real gap found while re-enriching this section: only counts below 1 were refused, so a p2c of 1 reduced PBKDF2 to a single HMAC.

should_policy is strict, so the RECOMMENDED floor is enforced rather than logged, and the reason is concrete: p2c travels in the token, so whoever writes it chooses how much a guess costs the attacker who later obtains it. What this module generates -- defaultPBES2Count, 600,000 -- is far above the floor, which was written in 2015 and is not a target now; that is this module's judgement rather than the RFC's and is recorded as such.

The count is bounded above as well, at maximumPBES2Count (10,000,000), with a distinct error. RFC 7518 states no ceiling, but a recipient obeying an arbitrary p2c will compute however many HMACs a sender asked for; RFC 8725 section 3.9 makes the general point about attacker-controlled parameters.

source.text: The number of octets in the input key K MUST be the sum of MAC_KEY_LEN and ENC_KEY_LEN.

requirements.condition: AES_CBC_HMAC_SHA2 content encryption is performed
requirements.behavior: require the input key K to be exactly MAC_KEY_LEN plus ENC_KEY_LEN octets
requirements.observable_effect: a CEK of any other length is refused rather than split anyway
requirements.oracle:
jwa.AESCBCHMACSHA2.keys returns jwa.ErrInvalidKeySize unless len(cek) == hash.Size() -- 32, 48 and 64 octets for A128CBC-HS256, A192CBC-HS384 and A256CBC-HS512. Asserted at one octet either side of each and at zero. Splitting a shorter key would hand AES a key of the wrong size and a longer one would quietly discard the excess, and the second failure mode is the one a round-trip test would not catch.

That the split itself is right -- MAC key first, encryption key second, "the opposite order of the algorithm names" as section 5.2.2.1 puts it -- is checked against RFC 7518 Appendix B, whose three vectors this module reproduces. Nothing in the standard library implements this composition, so unlike every other algorithm here it is assembled rather than delegated, and every way of assembling it wrongly still round-trips against itself.
inputs: CEKs of size-1, size+1 and 0 for each algorithm

notes: appears inside a figure/example block; may be illustrative, not normative

source.text: Use of an IV of size 96 bits is REQUIRED with this algorithm.

requirements.condition: AES GCM content encryption is performed
requirements.behavior: use a 96-bit initialization vector
requirements.observable_effect: the JWE Initialization Vector is 12 octets for A128GCM, A192GCM and A256GCM
requirements.oracle: jwa.AESGCM.IVSize returns gcmIVSize (12) for all three, and jwe.Message.Encrypt draws exactly that many octets. A received IV of any other length fails to decrypt. This module uses cipher.NewGCM rather than NewGCMWithRandomNonce deliberately: JWE carries the IV as its own part of the serialization, so the nonce is this package's to draw and publish.

source.text: The requested size of the Authentication Tag output MUST be 128 bits, regardless of the key size.

requirements.condition: AES GCM content encryption is performed
requirements.behavior: request a 128-bit authentication tag regardless of key size
requirements.observable_effect: the JWE Authentication Tag is 16 octets for all three AES GCM algorithms
requirements.oracle: jwa.AESGCM.Encrypt splits Seal's output at gcmTagSize (16) octets from the end. All three key sizes are asserted, since "regardless of the key size" is the operative clause and an implementation that scaled the tag with the key would interoperate with itself perfectly.

source.section_title: Parameters for Elliptic Curve Public Keys
source.text: The following members MUST be present for all Elliptic Curve public keys:

requirements.behavior: include crv and x on every Elliptic Curve public key
requirements.observable_effect: an EC jwk.Key marshals to an object carrying kty, crv and x, and decoding one that omits crv or x fails with jwk.MissingRequiredParameterError
requirements.oracle: Marshal an EC public key and assert crv and x are present. Decode documents with each of them removed in turn and assert a *jwk.MissingRequiredParameterError naming the missing one.
inputs: the same document with crv removed

source.section_title: Parameters for Elliptic Curve Public Keys
source.text: The following member MUST also be present for Elliptic Curve public keys for the three curves defined in the following section:

requirements.behavior: include y as well on public keys for P-256, P-384 and P-521
requirements.observable_effect: an EC jwk.Key on any of the three curves marshals with a y member, and decoding one without y fails
requirements.oracle: For each of P-256, P-384 and P-521, marshal a public key and assert y is present; decode the same document with y removed and assert a *jwk.MissingRequiredParameterError naming y.
inputs: public keys on each of the three curves

source.text: The length of this octet string MUST be the full size of a coordinate for the curve specified in the "crv" parameter.

requirements.behavior: encode x at the full coordinate width of the curve named by crv
requirements.observable_effect: the octets x decodes to number exactly ceil(bits/8) for the curve -- 32 for P-256, 48 for P-384, 66 for P-521 -- with leading zeros retained
requirements.oracle: Marshal public keys on each of P-256, P-384 and P-521 and assert the base64url-decoded x is 32, 48 and 66 octets respectively. 66 for P-521 is the case worth naming: its 521-bit coordinates round up to 66 octets, which is what the section calls the full size.
inputs: public keys on each of the three curves

source.text: The length of this octet string MUST be the full size of a coordinate for the curve specified in the "crv" parameter.

requirements.behavior: encode y at the full coordinate width of the curve named by crv
requirements.observable_effect: the octets y decodes to number exactly ceil(bits/8) for the curve -- 32 for P-256, 48 for P-384, 66 for P-521 -- with leading zeros retained
requirements.oracle: Marshal public keys on each of P-256, P-384 and P-521 and assert the base64url-decoded y is 32, 48 and 66 octets respectively. 66 for P-521 is the case worth naming: its 521-bit coordinates round up to 66 octets, which is what the section calls the full size.
inputs: public keys on each of the three curves

source.section_title: Parameters for Elliptic Curve Private Keys
source.text: In addition to the members used to represent Elliptic Curve public keys, the following member MUST be present to represent Elliptic Curve private keys.

requirements.behavior: include d to represent an Elliptic Curve private key
requirements.observable_effect: marshalling an *ecdsa.PrivateKey produces a d member alongside the public ones
requirements.oracle: Marshal an EC private key and assert d is present, and that jwk.Key.Public() strips it. The second half matters as much as the first: d is what makes the document private.

source.text: The length of this octet string MUST be ceiling(log-base-2(n)/8) octets (where n is the order of the curve).

requirements.behavior: encode d at ceiling(log-base-2(n)/8) octets, n being the curve order
requirements.observable_effect: the octets d decodes to number exactly the curve's coordinate width -- 32, 48 and 66 for P-256, P-384 and P-521
requirements.oracle: Marshal private keys on each of the three curves and assert the decoded d is 32, 48 and 66 octets. For these three curves the order and the field are of the same bit length, so this width coincides with the coordinate width tested for x and y.
inputs: private keys on each of the three curves

source.text: The following members MUST be present for RSA public keys.

requirements.behavior: include n and e on every RSA public key
requirements.observable_effect: an RSA jwk.Key marshals with n and e, and decoding one that omits either fails with jwk.MissingRequiredParameterError
requirements.oracle: Marshal an RSA public key and assert n and e are present; decode documents with each removed in turn and assert a *jwk.MissingRequiredParameterError naming it.

source.text: For instance, when representing the value 65537, the octet sequence to be base64url-encoded MUST consist of the three octets [1, 0, 1]; the resulting representation for this value is "AQAB".

requirements.condition: the exponent being represented is 65537
requirements.behavior: encode the exponent 65537 as the three octets [1, 0, 1], that is "AQAB"
requirements.observable_effect: the e member of a marshalled RSA key with the usual public exponent is exactly the string "AQAB"
requirements.oracle: Marshal an RSA key generated with crypto/rsa's default exponent and assert e equals "AQAB" exactly. This is the RFC's own worked value, so it is a published test vector rather than a restatement of the encoding rule.
inputs: a 2048-bit RSA key with public exponent 65537

source.text: The parameter "d" is REQUIRED for RSA private keys.

requirements.behavior: include d to represent an RSA private key
requirements.observable_effect: marshalling an *rsa.PrivateKey produces a d member
requirements.oracle: Marshal an RSA private key and assert d is present, and that Public() removes it.

source.text: The others enable optimizations and SHOULD be included by producers of JWKs representing RSA private keys.

requirements.behavior: include the CRT optimisation parameters p, q, dp, dq and qi when producing an RSA private JWK
requirements.observable_effect: a marshalled RSA private key carries all five alongside d
requirements.oracle: Marshal an RSA private key and assert p, q, dp, dq and qi are all present. The level is SHOULD, and this implementation does include them, so the test asserts the recommended behaviour directly rather than reporting advisory.

source.text: If the producer includes any of the other private key parameters, then all of the others MUST be present, with the exception of "oth", which MUST only be present when more than two prime factors were used.

requirements.condition: the producer includes any of the other private key parameters
requirements.behavior: include all of the other private key parameters when including any of them, oth excepted
requirements.observable_effect: the marshalled form carries the whole group p, q, dp, dq, qi or none of it -- never a proper subset

compound_review.rationale: the oth clause is a cross-reference to RFC7518-S6_3_2_7-R01 through R04, which carry it; this requirement holds only the all-or-none rule for the other private parameters

requirements.oracle: Marshal an RSA private key and assert the five members are either all present or all absent. The requirement is addressed to the producer, which is the side under test here; as a consumer this package is permitted to be, and is, more tolerant -- a document carrying only some of them decodes to a key holding just the public half rather than being rejected.

notes: Checked against the implementation as a consumer too: a document with d and p but no q, dp, dq or qi decodes without error to a *rsa.PublicKey. That is not a violation -- the sentence binds the producer -- but it is worth recording that the private half is dropped silently.

source.text: When only two primes have been used (the normal case), this parameter MUST be omitted.

requirements.condition: only two primes have been used
requirements.behavior: omit oth when only two primes were used
requirements.observable_effect: a marshalled two-prime RSA private key carries no oth member
requirements.oracle: Marshal an ordinary two-prime RSA private key and assert the object has no oth member at all -- absent, not present and empty.

source.text: When three or more primes have been used, the number of array elements MUST be the number of primes used minus two.

requirements.condition: three or more primes have been used
requirements.behavior: give oth as many elements as there are primes beyond the first two
requirements.rationale: This package refuses RSA keys of more than two primes in both directions, per the escape -R03 grants a consumer that does not support them, so it never produces an oth member whose length could be checked. Testing this would mean first implementing multi-prime support.

notes: Excluded as a consequence of the deliberate scope limit recorded in -R03.

source.text: If the consumer of a JWK does not support private keys with more than two primes and it encounters a private key that includes the "oth" parameter, then it MUST NOT use the key.

requirements.condition: the consumer does not support private keys of more than two primes and meets one carrying oth
requirements.behavior: not use a private key carrying oth when it does not support keys of more than two primes
requirements.observable_effect: decoding a JWK carrying a non-empty oth fails with jwk.ErrMultiPrimeKey rather than yielding a key built from the two primes it did understand
requirements.oracle: Decode a well formed RSA private JWK with an oth array of one element in the object form section 6.3.2.7 defines -- {"r":...,"d":...,"t":...} -- and assert an error wrapping jwk.ErrMultiPrimeKey. Writing the fixture in the RFC's object form rather than in whatever this package once emitted is the point: what must be refused is a conformant document describing a key this package cannot use.
inputs: an RSA private JWK carrying a one-element oth array

notes: Verified before the oracle was written: this package previously encoded oth as an array of bare base64url strings rather than of objects, so it both produced a document no conformant consumer could read and silently accepted its own malformed form. It now declines multi-prime keys on both paths, which is what this section licenses.

source.text: Each array element MUST be an object with the following members.

requirements.behavior: make each element of oth an object carrying r, d and t
requirements.rationale: Same reason as -R02: this package produces no oth member at all, having declined multi-prime keys outright. The consumer half of this requirement -- that a document using the object form is understood well enough to be refused rather than mis-parsed -- is what -R03 tests.

notes: Excluded as a consequence of the deliberate scope limit recorded in -R03.

source.text: An "alg" member SHOULD also be present to identify the algorithm intended to be used with the key, unless the application uses another means or convention to determine the algorithm used.

requirements.condition: the application does not use another means or convention to determine the algorithm
requirements.behavior: include an alg member on a symmetric key to identify the algorithm it is for
requirements.observable_effect: jwk.WithAlgorithm sets an alg member that survives a round trip, letting a producer follow the recommendation; the sentence's own escape clause means a key without one is still conformant
requirements.oracle: Marshal an oct key built with jwk.WithAlgorithm(jwa.HS256()) and assert alg is "HS256", and that it decodes back to the same algorithm. The requirement is on the producer of a JWK rather than on this library, and it carries an explicit escape ("unless the application uses another means or convention"), so what is tested is that the library makes compliance expressible.
inputs: an oct key with an algorithm set

source.text: In accordance with this rule, AES GCM MUST NOT be used with the same key value more than 2^32 times.

requirements.actor: application, over the lifetime of a key
actor_candidates: application, over the lifetime of a key
requirements.condition: one AES GCM key is used for many encryptions
requirements.behavior: not exceed 2^32 invocations with it
requirements.observable_effect: none this module can observe: it holds no state across calls and no count of a key's use
requirements.rationale:
The bound is over the lifetime of a key, across every process that ever uses it. This module is stateless with respect to key material -- a key arrives as an argument and is forgotten when the call returns -- so there is nowhere to keep a counter and nothing to compare it against. Enforcing it would require the library to own key storage, which it deliberately does not.

Recorded rather than quietly dropped: an application using "dir" or a long-lived A*GCMKW key needs to know the limit exists. The observable half of section 8.4 -- that this module never itself reuses an IV -- is asserted at RFC7518-S8_4-R02.

source.text: An IV value MUST NOT ever be used multiple times with the same AES GCM key.

requirements.condition: AES GCM is used, for content encryption or for key wrapping
requirements.behavior: never use one IV value twice with the same key
requirements.observable_effect: every encryption draws a fresh IV, and no call accepts one from the caller
requirements.oracle:
Two encryptions under one key produce different IVs, asserted for A128GCM content encryption and for A128GCMKW key wrapping, and across many repetitions rather than two. Structurally, jwa.AESGCMKeyWrap.WrapKey draws its IV internally and jwe.Message.Encrypt draws the content IV per message, so no caller can supply one twice; for multi-recipient messages the key wrap IV is drawn per call rather than per message, since wrapping one CEK twice under one key with one IV would repeat the keystream and expose the CEK.

Assumption, labelled: this tests freshness, not the birthday bound. Random 96-bit IVs collide with probability that grows with the square of the message count, which is the same fact section 8.4's 2^32 limit is about and which RFC7518-S8_4-R01 records as not-testable here. A test asserting distinctness over a feasible number of samples cannot distinguish a correct implementation from one with a slightly weakened random source, and this oracle does not claim to.
inputs: many encryptions under one key, for A128GCM and A128GCMKW
open_questions: No negative case exists for this prohibition, and one cannot be written from outside the package: there is no API through which a caller can supply an IV, which is precisely how the rule is enforced. The strategy is therefore a property over repeated encryptions rather than a refusal, and the structural argument -- that both draw sites call crypto/rand and neither reads a caller value -- is what the property stands in for.

source.section_title: Reusing Key Material when Encrypting Keys
source.text: It is NOT RECOMMENDED to reuse the same entire set of key material (Key Encryption Key, Content Encryption Key, Initialization Vector, etc.) to encrypt multiple JWK or JWK Set objects, or to encrypt the same JWK or JWK Set object multiple times.

requirements.condition: several objects are encrypted
requirements.behavior: not reuse the same entire set of key material across them
requirements.observable_effect: every encryption draws a fresh CEK and IV, so no two messages share the whole set even under one key
requirements.oracle:
Encrypting the same plaintext twice under one key produces different ciphertexts, for every key management algorithm except "dir". The CEK is drawn per message by jwa.GenerateContentEncryptionKey and the IV per message by jwe.Message.Encrypt, so the set as a whole differs even where the Key Encryption Key does not.

The exception is "dir" and it is the honest one: RFC 7518 section 4.5 makes the shared symmetric key the CEK, so the CEK is reused by construction and only the IV varies. That is what the mode is, not a defect in this implementation, and section 8.2's warning about key lifetimes is the reason jwa.Direct's doc comment points at it. should_policy is strict, so this is asserted rather than logged; "dir" is asserted separately, as varying the IV alone.
inputs: two encryptions of one plaintext under one key, per algorithm

source.text: It is RECOMMENDED that a password used for "PBES2-HS256+A128KW" be no shorter than 16 octets and no longer than 128 octets and a password used for "PBES2-HS512+A256KW" be no shorter than 32 octets and no longer than 128 octets long.

requirements.condition: a password is chosen for PBES2
requirements.behavior: keep it within the recommended length for the algorithm
requirements.observable_effect: encrypting with a password outside the range fails with jwa.ErrWeakPassword; decrypting one is unaffected
requirements.oracle:
jwa.PBES2.WrapKey returns jwa.ErrWeakPassword outside the range -- 16 to 128 octets for PBES2-HS256+A128KW and 32 to 128 for PBES2-HS512+A256KW, which are the two the RFC names. Both boundaries are asserted, so the check cannot pass by refusing everything. This was a real gap: any password of any length was previously accepted.

Applied when producing and not when consuming. The recommendation is addressed to whoever chooses the password, and that choice is made on the producing side, where refusing costs nothing but a better password; refusing on the receiving side would reject a message the recipient is entitled to read without making anyone's password stronger. The same asymmetry this module applies to "zip" and to RFC 7797's "b64", and the receiving half is asserted too -- a short password reaching DecryptKey never yields ErrWeakPassword.

Assumption, labelled: the RFC names bounds for PBES2-HS256+A128KW and PBES2-HS512+A256KW only. PBES2-HS384+A192KW sits between them and takes an interpolated floor of 24 octets, which is this module's reading rather than the RFC's text.
inputs: passwords at 0, 1, minimum-1, minimum, 128 and 129 octets, per algorithm

source.text: Passwords obtained from users are likely to require preparation and normalization to account for differences of octet sequences generated by different input devices, locales, etc. It is RECOMMENDED that applications perform the steps outlined in [PRECIS] to prepare a password supplied directly by a user before performing key derivation and encryption.

requirements.condition: a password is obtained from a user
requirements.behavior: apply the PRECIS OpaqueString profile before using it
requirements.observable_effect: none this module can observe: it receives octets and cannot tell prepared ones from unprepared

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

requirements.rationale:
PRECIS OpaqueString preparation (RFC 7613) is a Unicode operation requiring the width-mapping, normalization and disallowed-code-point tables. This module has zero dependencies and the standard library does not provide them, so implementing it here would mean either taking a dependency or vendoring Unicode tables that go stale.

More to the point, it is the wrong layer. jwa.PBES2 takes the password as []byte -- the API fact also recorded at RFC7518-S4_8-R01, and checkable in the signature rather than taken on that requirement's word -- so the caller has already decided what octets the password is, and preparing them afterwards would be second-guessing a decision already made with more context. The requirement is recorded as the application's rather than dropped, so the boundary stays visible to anyone reading the coverage report.

       MAC_KEY_LEN and ENC_KEY_LEN.  The values of these parameters are
       specified by the Authenticated Encryption algorithms in Sections
       5.2.3 through 5.2.5.  Note that the MAC key comes before the
       encryption key in the input key K; this is in the opposite order
       of the algorithm names in the identifier "AES_CBC_HMAC_SHA2".

the Additional Authenticated Data A,
          the Initialization Vector IV,
          the ciphertext E computed in the previous step, and
          the octet string AL defined above.

The string MAC_KEY is used as the MAC key.  We denote the output
       of the MAC computed in this step as M.  The first T_LEN octets of
       M are used as T.

MAC_KEY = initial MAC_KEY_LEN octets of K,
